Starting from a compatible cycle, choose a primitive at stage zero; lift it to the next stage, then correct the resulting cycle in the acyclic restriction kernel. Induction produces compatible primitives at all stages. This proves homotopical projectivity for the complete direct-sum bar resolution even when its suspended letters are negative.

For two algebras \(R,T\), use their tensor resolution, filtered by total bar length. Its augmentation has the tensor contraction and it has the same projectivity proof. The actual extended shuffle is a chain map of these two resolutions: the internal-letter identities are the graded cancellations of C.34.2, and its root identities are the two equal sign exponents in C.39.14. They likewise hold for degree-zero ordinary letters. Its map on augmentations is the identity. Its cone is acyclic and homotopically projective, so its identity is null-homotopic by applying that mapping property to the cone itself. The resulting \(R\otimes T\)-linear contraction remains a contraction after augmentation tensor. Thus the resulting actual reduced shuffle is a quasi-isomorphism. This is the complete free-resolution argument, rather than a convergence assertion for a negative bar-length spectral sequence.

Apply it to \(\mathcal U^{\otimes n}\) and \(kI\), and also use the already proved \(n\)-factor shuffle. Normalize the mapping contraction of \(\mathcal U^{\otimes n}\otimes kI\) by tensoring the chosen contraction of \(\mathcal U^{\otimes n}\) with each degree-zero index-arrow line. Its transferred model is exactly \(\mathcal M_n\otimes kI\): every tree term in the transfer has the same \(\mathcal U^{\otimes n}\) contraction and composition term, multiplied by the composite of its index arrows. The latter have degree zero, so add no interchange signs. Scalar identity inputs are normalized as in A.3.1.1. In particular a pure index word has zero homotopy and its ordinary index composition.

Let \(P_{n,I}\) be the resulting actual bar projection. The desired map is
\[
 \sigma_{n,I}
   =P_{n,I}\operatorname{sh}_2
       \left((\operatorname{sh}_n I_1^{\otimes n})\otimes1_{D_I}\right).
 \tag{C.42.3}
\]
Every map here is a chain coalgebra map. The bar inclusion and projection have the finite wordwise contraction of A.3.1.1 and C.35.1, so are quasi-isomorphisms. The shuffle just proved is a quasi-isomorphism, and split finite tensor products preserve it. This proves (C.42.1).

If all index factors are identity arrows at one index object, (C.42.3) is exactly the definition of \(\sigma_n\). On a pure index word, \(I_1\) contributes only its scalar coaugmentations, the shuffle is that same word, and \(P_{n,I}\) is the identity just checked. This proves both restrictions, without presuming naturality of unrelated minimal-model choices.

For the bounds on \(B(\mathcal M_n\otimes kI)\), its ordinary reduced letters have either positive degree at least two, or degree zero on a strict index arrow. If there are \(r_+\) positive letters and \(r_0\) zero-degree letters, then \(r_0\le H_I\). Their suspended degree is at least \(r_+-r_0\), while the height jump is at least \(r_0\). Consequently \(W\ge r_+\), and the total length is at most \(W+H_I\). The same argument applies to \(B(\mathcal U^{\otimes n}\otimes kI)\). On the tensor source, positive \(C\)-letters have suspended degree at least one and (C.42.2) bounds its index letters. This gives the same bound there.

At fixed \(D\), the height range bounds the degree above by \(D\) and below by \(-H_I\). The bound on word length then bounds every ordinary positive letter degree. There are finitely many index arrows and selected object labels, and the mapping spaces are degreewise finite. Thus the windows are finite. Cuts split degrees and heights additively; each piece has nonnegative weight by the same argument, so the windows are subcoalgebras. All comparison maps have degree zero and fixed endpoints, hence preserve \(W\). All coderivations have degree one and fixed endpoints, hence raise it by one. ∎

#### C.42.2. The weighted recovery of the native tree diagram

**Theorem C.42.2.1.** Take the actual rational ordered-tree functor graph of C.33.3 for finitely many arities and object labels, with its original coherent finite-frame contraction comparisons. The source core at arity \(n\) can be chosen as \(\mathcal M_n\otimes kT_n\), retaining its whole index. There is an actual common-core graph obtained by replacing that source bar by \(C^{\otimes n}\otimes D_{T_n}\), using \(\sigma_{n,T_n}\), and retaining \(C\) as the common output core.

Its graph comparison and its cobar comparison are quasi-isomorphisms on every corner. They retain the original tree-indexed enhanced functor diagram and all its transferred index-chain components. The same assertion applies to a full finite directed nested graph with such index-decorated cores, nonnegative minimal central mapping spaces, and all its actual several-cross operations.

**Proof.** First choose the source contractions before transferring the full graph. The enhanced input of C.33.3 is the rational tensor generator category tensored with \(kT_n\). Replace its tensor generator core by the positive \(\mathcal U^{\otimes n}\), using C.34's actual equivalence. Its index remains unchanged. The contraction chosen in C.42.1 gives the exact source model \(\mathcal M_n\otimes kT_n\).

Choose the target core contraction once and choose the cross mapping contractions after those source choices. The full graph transfer restricts to the already chosen source and target transfers on their pure core words. Its cross mapping cohomology is the actual \(\operatorname{Hom}(F_t\mathbf P,Q)\) of C.33.5, nonnegative, even and degreewise finite by C.33.1. Its higher operations retain the native coherent diagram because the transferred bar map is the whole original graph map. This uses the actual graph construction of C.33.2–C.33.3, rather than deducing a natural-transformation complex from the degrees of an object's mappings.

Apply C.40.1's path construction with the chain coalgebra maps \(f_i=\sigma_{n_i,I_i}\) on the decorated inputs and the identity on the output. Its proof of coassociativity, coderivation uniqueness, \(QD_A=D_BQ\) and \(D_A^2=0\) uses the finite path cuts and central projections; it does not assume positivity of a pure core run. Those exact proofs therefore apply here. In particular the path differential still has its operations consuming several cross letters and any intervening index runs.

Choose a total graph height strictly increasing on every strict index arrow and every cross arrow. For the native fixed-arity tree graph use the height of C.31.2 on its source and place its target one step above its maximum. For a finite collection of nested components, separate their level height ranges by constants. No reverse arrow is introduced. Let its range be \(H\), and define
\[
 W(w)=|w|+h(\text{left endpoint})-h(\text{right endpoint}).
 \tag{C.42.4}
\]
Every pure core piece has nonnegative weight, by C.42.1. A central cross letter \(sN\) has degree \(|N|-1\), with \(|N|\ge0\), and its endpoint height jump \(d\) is at least one. It too has nonnegative weight.

Filter the graph by cross count at most \(q\), where \(q\le H\). A grafting term cannot increase this count. On its fixed-count quotient only pure core differentials and one-cross module operations remain.

The ordinary central-degree filtration of C.40.2 no longer suffices: consuming a suspended degree-zero index arrow may leave the ordinary central degree unchanged. Instead use the descending filtration by
\[
 \nu=\sum_{\text{central cross letters}}
              \bigl(|N|+\Delta h_{\text{cross}}\bigr).
 \tag{C.42.5}
\]
A one-cross operation consuming left and right core pieces of summed cohomological degree \(a\) and summed height jump \(e\) changes the ordinary central degree by \(a+1\), since it is a degree-one suspended Taylor operation. Its output cross letter absorbs those same endpoint jumps, so its change of \(\nu\) is
\[
             a+1+e=W(\text{consumed cores})+1\ge1.
 \tag{C.42.6}
\]
Bare central unary operations vanish by minimality. Thus this is a subcomplex filtration and its associated differential acts only on the pure core slots.

On each associated quotient the graph map \(Q\) is the tensor of the actual quasi-isomorphisms \(f_i\), with the fixed central coefficient spaces. It is a quasi-isomorphism by C.42.1 and the split coefficient contraction of C.30.1. All summands retain their core endpoints, so their fixed \(\nu\) values remain the same in this tensor assertion.

For a path with \(q\) crosses, degrees and endpoint height jumps telescope to
\[
 W(w)=\sum_{\text{core slots}}W(\text{core slot})+\nu-q.
 \qquad 0\le\nu\le W(w)+q.
 \tag{C.42.7}
\]
In a fixed cohomological degree \(r\), \(W(w)\le r+H\); the same bound holds in its incoming degree. The \(\nu\) filtration is therefore finite there. Associated cone acyclicity can be eliminated finitely, as in C.39.4: solve the cycle's first nonzero filtration component, subtract that boundary, and repeat until the bounded filtration ends. This proves \(Q\) a quasi-isomorphism on the cross-count quotient. Induction on the finite cross-count filtration proves it on the full graph.

We supply the cobar and recovery bounds in the presence of an index. A reduced coalgebra element with zero height jump has degree at least one, because its nonempty core letters are positive and it has no cross or strict index arrow. A reduced element with positive jump \(d\) has degree at least \(-d\), because its weight is nonnegative. In a composable cobar word of \(r\) generators, let \(a\) have positive jump. Then \(a\le H\), and the sum of their jumps is at most \(H\). After desuspension that word's degree is at least
\[
 2(r-a)+a-H\ge2r-2H.
 \tag{C.42.8}
\]
The descending cobar-length filtration is consequently finite in every fixed degree and its incoming degree. Its associated map is a finite balanced tensor of the reduced cornerwise quasi-isomorphisms \(Q\). The split contraction and finite cone-elimination proof of C.39.4 proves \(\Omega Q\) is a quasi-isomorphism.

For a bar-cobar unit with \(r\) original coalgebra elements, their summed degrees are at least \(r-2H\). Formula (C.39.17) then bounds \(r\le t+2H\) in degree \(t\). The same explicit first-cut contraction of C.39.4 applies at every \(r\ge2\), including its internal signs. Its first quotient is the original coalgebra. This proves the units are quasi-isomorphisms.

We also verify recovery of the minimal graph itself. Its canonical \(A_\infty\) comparison to the cobar of its bar is the consecutive-block formula (C.34.3), applied to the whole directed graph. A word of \(r\) original ordinary arrows has at most \(H\) height-increasing arrows; all other reduced arrows have degree at least two. With \(v\ge1\) cobar blocks its degree is at least \(r-2H+v\). Thus the filtration by original arrow count is finite in each fixed degree. On a fixed-\(r\) quotient, splitting the \(r-1\) possible cuts is the exact exterior complex contracted in C.34.4. At \(r=1\) the comparison's first component is the original arrow; every \(r\ge2\) quotient contracts. The remaining higher bar operations lower \(r\), and minimality makes its original unary differential zero. Finite cone elimination proves that first component is a cornerwise quasi-isomorphism. It gives the required actual \(A_\infty\) equivalence; no strict counit from a cobar to a non-dg minimal category is assumed.

These are maps of the entire graph. Their core restrictions are the specified source/output equivalences, and their cross restrictions are the complete represented module comparisons. C.33.2's evaluation consequently recovers the native enhanced functor and its tree-indexed components. Index words of all lengths through the actual finite tree bound are retained. Their identities are the corresponding components of the full square-zero and chain coalgebra equations; no higher component is set to zero by an objectwise uniqueness argument.

Finally (C.42.7) bounds central ordinary degrees and the total positive core weight. The number of zero-degree index letters and cross letters is at most \(H\). Thus primitive-letter length is at most \(D+H\) in weight \(D\). There are finitely many profiles and coefficients at a finite corner. Cuts have nonnegative weights and all formulas retain their existing labels, so full finite corner and weight restrictions agree. This proves the remaining finite-system assertions. ∎

#### C.42.3. Coordinate groups and noncollapsing tree grafting

**Theorem C.42.3.1.** On a finite common-core graph of C.42.2 let \(g\) be a normalized core coordinate on \(C\). Require the whole-path coordinate \(G\) to have restrictions
\[
 G|_{C^{\otimes n}\otimes D_I}
            =g^{\otimes n}\otimes1_{D_I},
 \qquad G|_C=g.
 \tag{C.42.9}
\]
Together with fixed bare cross letters, factor labels and endpoint grades, these equations give a closed finite unitriangular coordinate group on its height-weight windows. Its operations are \((h,H)(g,G)=(hg,HG)\) and componentwise inverse. Full differential-comparison equations use inputs through weight \(D-1\) and outputs through \(D\); whenever a complete selected marked comparison has a point, its reduced solution variety is a target-stabilizer torsor in this actual group.

For positive ordered block sizes \(n_1,\ldots,n_m\), the tree grafting functor gives an actual index coalgebra map
\[
 \gamma_{\mathbf n}:D_{T_m}\otimes\bigotimes_i D_{T_{n_i}}
             \longrightarrow D_{T_N},\qquad N=\sum_i n_i.
 \tag{C.42.10}
\]
It preserves the summed height weight, regroups associatively, and commutes with all the coordinates (C.42.9). Unit insertion on the common tensor cores is the coaugmentation at the IC unit and likewise commutes strictly with the common core powers. These algebraic statements retain the native diagram of C.42.2; actual cross-arity and geometric unit comparison marks still require their complete module and higher covariance data.

**Proof.** An index bar is cofree on its strict index-arrow letters, with its given differential. The other pure factors are the same cofree \(C\)'s as in C.40.3. Their tensor cores and path sectors have the same total primitive-letter coradical filtration: the iterated reduced coproduct followed by the canonical factor-order projection recovers every original factor word and cross sequence with coefficient a Koszul unit. This is C.40.3's complete injectivity argument applied also to the index factor.

The prescribed index coordinate is the identity, and all other primitive and bare-cross leading coordinates are fixed as before. Thus every coordinate is the identity on each associated length piece. It is unitriangular. C.42.2 bounds that length by \(D+H\); the matrices and their inverses are finite. Degree-zero, endpoint-preserving maps preserve \(W\). Equation (C.42.9) uses only the degree window of \(g\) already retained: each \(C\) factor's positive degree is at most the total core weight. Its entries are polynomial products of entries of that one \(g\); the index entries are fixed constants.

Coalgebra, degree, leading-entry and restriction equations are closed polynomial equations. Composition gives \(h^{\otimes n}g^{\otimes n}=(hg)^{\otimes n}\) on the decorated source, with the same identity index map. The inverse is \((g^{-1})^{\otimes n}\otimes1\). These calculations and the finite length recursion prove the group assertion. Differential comparisons have exactly the bounded domains stated because differentials raise \(W\) by one. The quotient of two solutions commutes with the target differential on those same domains, while each target stabilizer carries a solution to a solution. This is the actual torsor calculation of C.40.3. Extra marks require their full bounded domains and the stated nonempty point hypothesis; neither is inferred from an unmarked graph comparison.

We verify (C.42.10), including the augmentation condition. Set \(T_1\) to be the one-leaf identity tree, a one-object category of height zero. For \(n\ge2\), represent a tree by its proper intervals as in C.31.1. Grafting replaces outer leaf \(i\) by an interval block \(J_i\) of \(n_i\) consecutive final leaves. Its proper intervals are the following disjoint kinds: the inner proper intervals inside the \(J_i\)'s; each seam interval \(J_i\) with \(n_i\ge2\), when \(m\ge2\); and the expansions of the outer proper intervals into unions of consecutive blocks.

Every variable interval determines its source unambiguously. Inner intervals are properly contained in one \(J_i\), while outer expanded intervals contain at least two blocks. The fixed seams are a third kind. Deleting any source variable interval therefore deletes a distinct proper target interval. Grafting is injective on its tree tuples and sends every nonidentity contraction to a nonidentity contraction. It is a functor because two successive deletions have the same union of deleted intervals. It therefore preserves the augmentation to scalar identity categories. Its actual reduced bar map is defined.

Define \(\gamma_{\mathbf n}\) by the shuffle into the bar of the product index category, followed by that bar grafting map. Its shuffle is a chain coalgebra map by the homogeneous-letter signs of C.34.2, valid also for the degree-zero index algebras by C.42.1. Its bar grafting map is a chain coalgebra map because it preserves arrow composition, identities and nonidentity arrows. This proves (C.42.10).

Give \(T_n\), \(n\ge2\), height \(n-2\) minus the number of proper intervals, and give \(T_1\) height zero. If \(m\ge2\), put \(r=\#\{i:n_i=1\}\). There are \(m-r\) fixed seam intervals, so the grafted height is
\[
 N-2-\#(\text{outer proper intervals})
       -\sum_i\#(\text{inner proper intervals})-(m-r).
 \tag{C.42.11}
\]
This is exactly the sum of the outer and inner heights, since
\(\sum_i\max(0,n_i-2)=N-2m+r\).
For \(m=1\) grafting is just the inner tree and has that same assertion. Hence endpoint height jumps agree. The shuffle preserves total suspended degree, and grafting does not alter the number of letters. Thus (C.42.10) preserves weight.

For nested grafting the final interval collections are identical in both orders: they are the same expanded outer intervals, seams and inner intervals. This proves strict associativity on index categories. The shuffle regrouping identity of C.34.2 consequently proves the same identity for their coalgebra maps. Regrouping \(C\)-factors also preserves their fixed order. Their single coordinate is \(g^{\otimes N}\), independently of grouping; the index coordinates are identities. This proves the strict covariance of the common-core/index maps.

Let \(e_{\mathbf1}\) be the group-like coaugmentation for the simple IC unit object. Its insertion in tensor slot \(r\) defines
\[
 j_r:C^{\otimes n}\longrightarrow C^{\otimes(n+1)},\qquad
 j_r(c_1\otimes\cdots\otimes c_n)
       =c_1\otimes\cdots\otimes e_{\mathbf1}\otimes\cdots\otimes c_n.
 \tag{C.42.12}
\]
The inserted element is closed, counital and group-like, so this is a chain coalgebra map preserving positive core degree. Normalized core coordinates fix it. Direct substitution gives \(g^{\otimes(n+1)}j_r=j_rg^{\otimes n}\), including \(n=0\). On finite retained windows these insertion equations use only existing degree-zero coefficient entries.

Positive-arity grafting and the common-core insertion are the maps just proved. A diagram deleting a nullary unit vertex can collapse a nonidentity index arrow to an identity. It is not covered by this augmented reduced-bar grafting proof, and must be retained through its actual unital functor/module diagram. Moreover (C.42.10)–(C.42.12) alone do not identify the two actual convolution modules under a grafting or supply their geometric unit transformation. C.41 gives the exact block-product sectors; their full covariance with the native C.42.2 diagram and its complete extension-field solution are still required. ∎

#### C.42.4. The height correction and a collapsed arrow

**Exercise C.42.4.1.** Let \(I\) have objects \(0<1<2\), arrows \(a:0\to1,b:1\to2,c:0\to2\) with \(ba=c\), and height \(h(i)=i\). Compute the differential and weight of \(sb|sa\). Adjoin an output \(y\) of height two and a degree-zero cross letter \(m:1\to y\), whose composition with \(a\) is a nonzero degree-zero cross letter \(m_a:0\to y\). Compute the change in the two central filtrations under \(sm|sa\mapsto -sm_a\).

**Solution.** Both suspended index arrows have degree minus one. Their bar product is
\[
 b_2(sb|sa)=-sc.
 \qquad W(sb|sa)=0,\quad W(sc)=1.
 \tag{C.42.13}
\]
The heights are the same total jump two, while the differential raises suspended degree from minus two to minus one. In the crossed calculation both ordinary central mappings have degree zero, so that degree does not increase at all. The original central height jump is \(2-1=1\), and the new one is \(2-0=2\). Thus \(\nu\) increases from one to two. The consumed core has degree minus one and height jump one, hence weight zero; its change \(W+1=1\) is exactly (C.42.6).

An associated quotient retaining only ordinary central degree would still contain this index action. The \(\nu\) quotient removes it while retaining the full action in the original graph. This is why the new filtration proves recovery without deleting native tree comparisons.

**Exercise C.42.4.2.** Let \(J\) have one nonidentity arrow \(a:0\to1\), and let \(F:J\to\{*\}\) send both objects to \(*\) and \(a\) to the identity. What fails if one tries to represent \(F\) by sending the reduced suspended arrow \(sa\) to zero? Compare the two maps after cobar and the bar-cobar counit.

**Solution.** There is no nonempty reduced target arrow: its target category is the scalar identity category. A reduced zero-arrow formula therefore kills \(sa\). After cobar it sends the generator \(t(sa)\) to zero. The source bar-cobar counit sends that generator to \(a\), whereas the actual functor sends \(a\) to \(1_*\). Thus the composites are
\[
 t(sa)\longmapsto0
 \qquad\text{and}\qquad
 t(sa)\longmapsto1_*.
 \tag{C.42.14}
\]
They differ already in degree zero. The original arrow lies in the kernel of the source identity augmentation; its image under \(F\) does not lie in the kernel of the target augmentation. Hence the augmented reduced-bar functor formula does not apply. An independently defined zero-arrow coalgebra map, when interpreted after cobar, represents a different functor.

This calculation does not obstruct the normalized unital \(A_\infty\) or represented-module construction of the actual \(F\). It identifies the exact additional datum needed when an index arrow collapses. Positive-arity grafting in C.42.3 was proved noncollapsing; the geometric nullary/unit diagrams must be handled with their actual unital maps.

![The native ordered-tree index keeps its negative suspended arrow degrees; weighted central height proves common-core graph recovery; positive grafting preserves the fixed index, while a collapsed arrow requires its actual unital map](assets/directed-tree-common-cores.png)

Theorem C.42.1.1 proves the actual index-decorated shuffle and finite height-weight windows. Theorem C.42.2.1 proves recovery of the complete native indexed graph using the central quantity in equations (C.42.5)–(C.42.7), including the full finite-height bar-cobar comparisons. Theorem C.42.3.1 proves the fixed-index coordinate group, augmentation-preserving positive grafting and common-core unit insertion. Exercises C.42.4.1–C.42.4.2 check the displayed negative degree, corrected filtration and collapsed-arrow distinction. Editable SVG source. Free background on the augmentation and bar conventions: [Keller, Introduction to A-infinity algebras and modules, Sections 3.5–3.6](https://arxiv.org/pdf/math/9910179).

### C.43. Canonical input squares and transfer preserving prescribed modules

Canonical bar-cobar units give a strictly natural common input. Separately chosen contraction inclusions need not have that property. We also transfer a full graph only after choosing its module contractions; this preserves the exact product maps in a comparison, rather than merely identifying the two product models afterwards.

#### C.43.1. A strictly natural common input

**Theorem C.43.1.1.** Let \(C,D\) be the positive IC bar coalgebras, and let \(g:C\to D\) be a normalized chain coalgebra map with its prescribed object map. Put \(U_C=\Omega C,U_D=\Omega D,q=\Omega g\). For a finite directed poset \(I\), define
\[
 \psi^C_{n,I}
   =\operatorname{sh}_{n+1}
        \bigl(\eta_C^{\otimes n}\otimes1_{D_I}\bigr):
 C^{\otimes n}\otimes D_I
              \longrightarrow B(U_C^{\otimes n}\otimes kI).
 \tag{C.43.1}
\]
Here the shuffle includes the index as its last factor, and \(D_I=B(kI)\). This is an actual chain coalgebra quasi-isomorphism and satisfies the strict equality
\[
 B(q^{\otimes n}\otimes1_{kI})\psi^C_{n,I}
       =\psi^D_{n,I}(g^{\otimes n}\otimes1_{D_I}).
 \tag{C.43.2}
\]
Its additional rectified input map is
\[
 \widehat\psi^C_{n,I}
   =\eta_{B(U_C^{\otimes n}\otimes kI)}\psi^C_{n,I}.
 \tag{C.43.3}
\]
It has that same strict square with input functor
\(\Omega B(q^{\otimes n}\otimes1_{kI})\).
These maps retain the fixed index, ordered regrouping, positive tree grafting and coaugmentation insertions. In particular their common input coordinates are literally the indicated tensor powers of \(g\).

**Proof.** The units are the actual iterated-coproduct maps (C.39.16), not an independently chosen minimal-model inclusion. Their naturality is the identity
\[
 B(\Omega g)\eta_C=\eta_Dg.
 \tag{C.43.4}
\]
Indeed on the component of bar length \(r\), both sides apply \(g\) to the \(r\) original pieces in the iterated coproduct of the input. The coproduct identity of \(g\) makes these the same tensor, including the graded signs. Their coefficient components are the prescribed identity maps. This proves the equality on the whole cofree bar.

The shuffle is natural under strict dg functors: applying such a functor to each embedded single-factor bar letter before or after a shuffle gives the same interleavings, with the same degrees and Koszul signs. Use (C.43.4) on each \(C\)-factor and the identity on the index factor. This proves (C.43.2) as an exact map equality.

C.39.4 proves \(\eta_C\) is a quasi-isomorphism and C.42.1 proves the actual index-decorated shuffle is one. The coefficient tensor contraction proves the finite tensor assertion. Their composite is therefore the stated quasi-isomorphism. Applying C.42.2's finite-height bar-cobar-unit bound to \(B(U_C^{\otimes n}\otimes kI)\) proves that the further unit in (C.43.3) is a quasi-isomorphism too. Naturality of that same unit, now under \(B(q^{\otimes n}\otimes1)\), gives the strict square for (C.43.3).

Ordered regrouping of shuffle words is C.34.2's actual regrouping identity. On index factors use the noncollapsing grafting maps proved in C.42.3; functor naturality and shuffle regrouping give the same maps in both orders. Inserting a common-core coaugmentation contributes only the closed group-like coefficient object to \(\eta\), and contributes no shuffle letter. Thus insertion commutes with (C.43.1) and its \(g\)-square, including the empty input. The same statement holds for graded permutations of the positive factors if those are retained as marked maps. All maps are of degree zero with fixed endpoints, so the height-weight windows of C.42.1 contain their outputs.

Consequently this is a permissible replacement of the original actual input model by quasi-equivalent common cores. It does not assert that the independently chosen \(\sigma_{n,I}\) of C.42.1 has a strictly natural square. C.35–C.36 retain the homotopies for that earlier choice. Here the natural square follows instead from the canonical unit and the actual shuffle themselves. ∎

#### C.43.2. Indexed functors retain their scalar outputs

**Theorem C.43.2.1.** Let \(R=U_C^{\otimes n}\otimes kI\) be the augmented dg input above, and let \(V\) be a unital dg target, allowing the finite additive image matrices of C.38.1. A normalized unital \(A_\infty\) functor from \(R\) to \(V\) has a strict dg representative
\[
 F^\sharp:\Omega B R\longrightarrow V
 \tag{C.43.5}
\]
which retains its full output components, including scalar identities. No augmentation compatibility of \(F\) is required.

For the graph-recovery assertion, suppose additionally that the target core is one of the augmented positive dg cores used above, with its scalar or prescribed finite-matrix coefficient category. The represented graph of \(F^\sharp\), pulled back on its target and source bars along their canonical maps and (C.43.3), then has the actual common-core indexed functor as its perfect-envelope interpretation. This construction retains an index arrow whose actual functor image is an identity.

**Proof.** Fix the image of each input object. On a reduced composable input bar word \(c\), the functor components determine a degree-one map \(\tau(c)\) into the full target mapping space. In the present suspension convention the complete functor equation is
\[
 d_V\tau(c)=\tau(b_Rc)
       -\sum_{\bar\Delta c}(-1)^{|c_{(1)}|}
                      \tau(c_{(1)})\tau(c_{(2)}).
 \tag{C.43.6}
\]
This is equivalently the normalized \(A_\infty\) equation: its first term applies each source differential or composition to a consecutive input block; its sum composes the two target outputs of a cut, with the degree-one twisting sign. All target outputs are in \(V\), including its coefficient identities.

Define (C.43.5) on each free cobar generator by \(tc\mapsto\tau(c)\), and extend by target composition and the prescribed object-unit maps. Its generator differential is exactly (C.39.15). Equation (C.43.6) therefore says it is a chain map on those generators. Its extension commutes with the full differential by the dg Leibniz rule, so is a dg functor. Conversely restriction of such a dg functor to the free generators gives (C.43.6).

The canonical \(A_\infty\) comparison \(R\to\Omega BR\) has Taylor component \(c\mapsto tc\), as in the consecutive-block construction of C.34.3. Composing it with the strict \(F^\sharp\) gives precisely \(\tau(c)\) on every reduced input word, including scalar outputs. Thus the composite is the original normalized functor itself. The finite-height cut proof of C.42.2 makes that canonical comparison a quasi-equivalence for this indexed input. This proves the representative assertion and its actual recovery, with the signs fixed by the already proved cobar formula.

Source scalar identities are handled by normalization and by the object-unit maps; they are not reduced bar letters. A scalar *output* of \(\tau\), however, is retained when the functor identifies the images of two input objects. This is allowed in a functor from the free source cobar to a unital target. It does not define a reduced augmented bar functor into \(BV\) when that scalar output violates the target augmentation. Thus (C.43.5) does not use the zero-output replacement disproved in C.42.4.2.

The indexed enhanced functors of C.33.3 admit these normalized unital components. To see this with the chosen cores, transport the original functor through the fixed mapping contractions as in A.3.1.1 and C.38.1, retaining its full object-image matrix maps. Compose its target model with the canonical \(A_\infty\) comparison from C.34.1. Normalization at ordinary unary identity arguments is the same side-condition normalization used there. Index arrows between distinct source objects remain reduced inputs; their output components are not projected away. This gives exactly the full \(\tau\) used above.

For this graph assertion, take the stated augmented positive target core and the genuine graph with source \(\Omega BR\), target \(V\), cross mappings \(\operatorname{Hom}_V(F^\sharp a,y)\), and right action by \(F^\sharp\). Its dg composition is associative and has the Leibniz rule because \(F^\sharp\) is a dg functor; the proof is the two-level instance of C.38.1. Its pure source and target cores are augmented separately, regardless of whether \(F^\sharp\) preserves their augmentations. The entire graph is therefore augmented over its scalar vertex identities: a cross composition still has different graph levels as endpoints and cannot land in that coefficient category.

Its bar is consequently a genuine chain coalgebra. The graph comparison after common-core pullback is the one-cross case of C.40.1, retaining the central unary differential and all scalar-output actions in the cross module. The canonical source maps (C.43.3) are quasi-isomorphisms, and the graph recovery is the finite-height comparison of C.42.2, or the represented-module evaluation of C.33.2 after those source equivalences. Thus its perfect envelope recovers the actual indexed enhanced functor. The constant image of a strict index arrow appears as its actual right cross action.

Only the input cores and their comparisons use augmented reduced bars here. The functor to the target uses the full unital twisting components. This distinction preserves the unit data without imposing a false augmentation condition. ∎

#### C.43.3. Transfer the modules before the full grafting graph

**Theorem C.43.3.1.** Let \(L\) be a finite directed path coalgebra with fixed pure cores and a full square-zero graph differential \(d\). On every one-cross module choose an actual normalized bicomodule contraction over the identity cores to a prescribed cofree minimal-central module. Whenever a one-cross module is a block product, choose the shifted product of the individual contractions in C.41.2.

These prescribed contractions extend to a whole-graph transfer fixing the cores. The transferred graph has exactly those one-cross modules and exactly those one-cross inclusion and projection maps; it also retains all several-cross operations and their transferred identities.

Suppose a full raw chain coalgebra comparison \(T:L\to L'\) is given over its prescribed core maps, retaining the same level and string labels, and has a block restriction equal to the shifted tensor of its individual one-cross comparisons \(T_i\). The transferred comparison has that same exact product restriction:
\[
 \overline T_P
    =\left(\bigotimes_i K(\overline T_i)\right)[1],
 \qquad
 \overline T_i=P_i'T_iI_i.
 \tag{C.43.7}
\]
If its core maps themselves and its bare central leading components are isomorphisms, it is a whole-path coalgebra isomorphism. The construction preserves finite full corners. With the positive common cores, it stays in the finite height-weight windows already proved.

**Proof.** Write \(d_{\rm mod}\) for the pure core differential together with every one-cross module operation, but with no operation merging two or more cross letters. The graph's restriction to a one-cross sector is a module differential. Its square is zero there, and it has the prescribed core coderivations. Extending these module operations to paths by their coactions defines a coderivation \(d_{\rm mod}\). On a fixed path this is the cotensor-product differential of its consecutive modules. The tensor differential cancellations prove its square is zero. Thus \(d_{\rm mod}^2=0\) on the entire graph.

Let \(I_i,P_i,H_i\) be the chosen module contractions, with \(E_i=I_iP_i\). These are already the full perturbed module maps of C.41.2, not just maps on bare central complexes. A path is the iterated cotensor of its one-cross modules over the intermediate cores, by C.39.1. Tensor the \(I_i\)'s and \(P_i\)'s on that cotensor. They stay in it because their two coactions are over the identity cores. Together with the identity on pure cores they give whole-path maps \(I,P\).

They are coalgebra maps. To check this, a path cut is either between two cross letters or inside one boundary core run. At a between-cross cut their tensors split into the two same tensors. At an inside-core cut the corresponding bicomodule coaction equation of the module map gives precisely those two pieces. These are every path cut, and establish the full coproduct equations. Their retraction identity is \(PI=1\), by the individual identities.

On a cotensor path set
\[
 H=\sum_j E_1\otimes\cdots\otimes E_{j-1}
                \otimes H_j\otimes1\otimes\cdots\otimes1,
 \tag{C.43.8}
\]
with its Koszul evaluation signs, and set \(H=0\) on pure cores. Each summand is a well-defined degree-minus-one cotensor map: the degree-sensitive coaction equations of \(H_j\) and the degree-zero equations of the other maps preserve the equalizer. The differential telescope of C.41.8 proves
\[
 d_{\rm mod}H+Hd_{\rm mod}=1-IP,\qquad
 H^2=PH=HI=0.
 \tag{C.43.9}
\]
It also proves the chain identities for \(I,P\) with the prescribed minimal-module differential.

The homotopy has the full cut identity
\[
 \Delta H=(H\otimes1+IP\otimes H)\Delta.
 \tag{C.43.10}
\]
For a cut between module positions, a summand whose homotopy position lies before that cut gives the first term, and one after it gives the second. For a cut through a boundary core run, use the corresponding left or right bicomodule equation. The preceding \(E_i\)'s give \(IP\) on the cut prefix; the remaining identities give the first term's cut suffix. If the cut is outside all crossed positions, the pure core homotopy is zero and the pure core retract is the identity, giving that same formula. Thus this argument checks every cut with the graded signs; it does not require the chosen module homotopies to act only on their bare central letters.

Put \(\delta=d-d_{\rm mod}\). Every nonzero term in it merges at least two cross letters to one, since all one-cross terms were included in \(d_{\rm mod}\). It strictly lowers cross count. The maps \(I,P,H\) preserve that count. At finite directed height there are at most \(H_{\rm lev}\) cross letters, so \(H\delta\) and \(\delta H\) are locally nilpotent with that uniform finite bound. The full transfer is therefore
\[
 I^\infty=(1+H\delta)^{-1}I,\quad
 P^\infty=P(1+\delta H)^{-1},\quad
 H^\infty=H(1+\delta H)^{-1}.
 \tag{C.43.11}
\]
Its differential is the prescribed module differential plus \(P\delta I^\infty\).

C.35.1's algebraic proof gives the contraction and square-zero identities. The cut identity (C.43.10) and the coderivation equation for \(\delta\) give the coalgebra identities by the finite cross-count recursion: substitute them in the inclusion and projection recursions; at each count, all differences from the required coproduct equation have smaller count, and vanish inductively. This is the same complete recursion as A.3.1.1 and C.41.3, now using cross count rather than total primitive length. C.36.1's computation gives the perturbed homotopy's nonlinear cut identity as well.

On the zero-cross and one-cross sectors, \(\delta\) is zero. Hence (C.43.11) restricts *exactly* to the initially prescribed core identities and module \(I_i,P_i,H_i\). The differential has exactly the chosen one-cross actions. On several-cross sectors it includes every perturbation term from the original grafting operations. The transferred square-zero equation gives all their higher compatibility identities. No merging term has been dropped.

For two graphs the transferred comparison is
\(\overline T=P'^\infty T I^\infty\).
It is a chain coalgebra map by the identities just proved. On its one-cross sector it is \(P_i'T_iI_i\), since both infinite maps restrict exactly there. On a block-product sector the chosen inclusions and projections are the shifted products of their one-block counterparts. Its raw \(T_P\) is that same shifted product by hypothesis. Their three consecutive products are therefore precisely (C.43.7), with the shift signs of C.41.6. This proves the exact product assertion for the comparison itself.

This last calculation requires the supplied full \(T\), including all its several-cross compatibility components. It does not infer them from the individual \(T_i\)'s. Conversely it does not need an independently chosen whole-graph contraction to commute with that product.

For the inverse, first factor out the given invertible core and bare central leading maps. On the remaining path coalgebra, the normalized map is the identity on its primitive-length associated quotients, by the iterated-cut injection proved in C.40.3. Its difference from the identity lowers that length. The finite recursive inverse consequently preserves the coproduct and endpoints; it commutes with the differentials by the original chain equation. With an index use C.42.3's same length argument. Thus the comparison is the asserted actual isomorphism.

Every cotensor, map, cut and operation uses its existing endpoint and intermediate labels. Full finite corners therefore restrict the same formulas. In positive common cores, the initial module maps preserve degree and endpoints, while their homotopies have degree minus one. They preserve, respectively lower, the height weight of C.40.2. Each original grafting term has degree one with the same endpoints. The finite sums in (C.43.11) have the same degree and endpoint bounds. This verifies the retained window assertion.

The theorem supplies a transfer preserving prescribed products and a genuine comparison when its full raw comparison is supplied. The complete native cross-arity/unit comparison and its arithmetic point in the whole marked presentation remain additional required constructions before rational strong monoidal descent. ∎

#### C.43.4. Scalar index action and an actual higher graph projection

**Exercise C.43.4.1.** For \(I=(0<1<2)\), keep the arrows \(a,b,c=ba\) from C.42.4.1. Define a unital functor on \(\Omega B(kI)\) by sending each one-letter cobar generator \(t(sa),t(sb),t(sc)\) to the identity of its one-object target, and its two-letter generator to zero. Check its differential on \(t(sb|sa)\). Which missing datum of the reduced zero-arrow map has been restored?

**Solution.** The generator has degree minus one, and its differential is
\[
 d_\Omega t(sb|sa)=-t(sc)+t(sb)t(sa).
 \tag{C.43.12}
\]
Indeed its internal bar term is \(-sc\), while the splitting coefficient in (C.39.15) is \(-(-1)^{|sb|}=+1\). Applying the proposed functor gives \(-1+1=0\), the differential of its zero image. The one-letter generators are closed. Extending on all products therefore gives the actual dg functor.

Its twisting component on each suspended index arrow is the scalar \(1\). This restores the actual index action which the reduced zero-arrow formula had removed. Scalar outputs belong to the full target in (C.43.6), even though they are absent from its reduced bar.

**Exercise C.43.4.2.** Take three graph levels with only scalar pure cores. In each adjacent cross complex use \(p_i\) in degree zero, \(x_i\) in degree one and \(y_i\) in degree two, with \(dx_i=y_i\), for \(i=10,21\). In the direct \(20\) corner take a closed \(q_{20}\) in degree two. The only nonzero two-cross product is \(x_{21}x_{10}=q_{20}\). Use \(h(y_i)=x_i\), projection to \(p_i\), and the identity contraction on \(q_{20}\). Compute the full transferred bar projection on \(sy_{21}|sx_{10}\).

**Solution.** This is a dg graph: the differential of its one nonzero product is zero, and the Leibniz terms \(y_{21}x_{10}-x_{21}y_{10}\) are both zero. No three-cross product is composable. Its graph has finite height two.

In the module-first contraction the ordered homotopy sends \(sy_{21}|sx_{10}\) to \(sx_{21}|sx_{10}\). The alternative homotopy term contains the projection of \(y_{21}\), hence vanishes. The actual bar grafting sends that result to \(sq_{20}\): its suspended multiplication sign is \((-1)^{|sx_{21}|}=+1\). This direct corner has zero homotopy. Since a graft reduces two crosses to one, all later perturbation terms vanish. Consequently
\[
 P^\infty(sy_{21}|sx_{10})
       =P(sy_{21}|sx_{10})-P\delta H(sy_{21}|sx_{10})
       =-sq_{20}.
 \tag{C.43.13}
\]
Both sides have suspended degree one. All central cohomology degrees in this example are even: they are the adjacent \(p_i\)'s and the direct \(q_{20}\). The nonzero higher projection is retained nevertheless. It is part of the whole-graph contraction and cannot be read off from the ordinary projection of the two adjacent cross complexes alone.

This finite dg graph checks the full projection formula; it is not identified with an IC mapping complex. C.43.3 proves the general assertion with its actual modules, products and several-cross operations.

Theorem C.43.1.1 proves the exact square and its quasi-isomorphism, including canonical rectification, index maps and unit insertions. Theorem C.43.2.1 proves the full-target unital twisting representative and its actual functor recovery. Theorem C.43.3.1 transfers the whole graph after its prescribed modules, retaining their exact products and all grafting. Exercises C.43.4.1–C.43.4.2 prove the scalar differential and higher graph projection displayed here. Editable SVG source. ### C.44. Formal unit vertices and finite execution indices

To retain unit comparisons, a nullary operation vertex must be distinguished from an external input leaf. A unary operation vertex is also retained until its identity comparison is recorded. Their contraction index has parallel arrows; replacing it by a poset would remove part of its actual coherence diagram.

#### C.44.1. The complete finite formal tree index

**Lemma C.44.1.1.** Fix \(n\ge0,L\ge1\). Let \(\mathcal T_{n,L}\) have as objects planar rooted trees with \(n\) ordered external input leaves and between one and \(L\) operation vertices. Every operation vertex may have any arity, including zero or one. An external input leaf is a separate kind of endpoint and is never contracted. A morphism remembers a selected set of original edges between operation vertices to contract, with the resulting planar quotient identified with its target.

These data define a finite category. Its only endomorphisms are identities; it can have parallel morphisms. Height \(h(t)=L-V(t)\), with \(V(t)\) its operation-vertex count, strictly increases on every nonidentity morphism. A strict morphism chain has length at most \(L-1\). The \(n\)-corolla is terminal, also for \(n=0,1\), and the augmented normalized nerve is contractible over \(\mathbf Z\). Its linear category over the characteristic-zero coefficient field has the finite relative resolution proved in C.31.2.

**Proof.** A planar rooted tree is specified recursively as an operation vertex with an ordered list of inputs, each an external leaf or another such operation tree. A zero-length list is a nullary operation vertex, not an external leaf. The root is always an operation vertex. External leaves acquire their fixed order from the planar input lists.

Counting all edges except the outgoing root edge gives
\[
 \sum_{\text{operation vertices }v}r(v)=n+V-1.
 \tag{C.44.1}
\]
The left side counts their input edges. The right side counts the \(n\) external-leaf edges and the \(V-1\) edges between operation vertices. In particular each arity is at most \(n+L-1\). The full ordinary tree has \(n+V\) nodes, if external leaves are counted as endpoints. There are only finitely many rooted ordered tree shapes with at most \(n+L\) nodes: encode them by their finite preorder lists of incoming arities, each bounded by \(n+L\). Marking which leaf endpoints are external leaves makes only finitely many further choices. Hence there are finitely many objects. A planar rooted tree has no nonidentity planar automorphism, by induction on its ordered child subtrees.

For a selected set \(E\) of operation edges, take the connected components of the subgraph formed by those edges and their incident operation vertices, including isolated vertices. Collapse each component to one operation vertex. Its ordered incoming edges are the old incoming edges whose other endpoints are outside that component, in their inherited planar order. A component containing \(a\) original operation vertices has \(a-1\) selected internal edges; its resulting arity is the sum of their arities minus \(a-1\), a nonnegative integer because it counts exactly those remaining input edges. External leaves are unchanged. The resulting graph is again a planar rooted tree with
\[
                    V(t/E)=V(t)-|E|.
 \tag{C.44.2}
\]
It still has at least one operation vertex. Thus its object belongs to the same category. Its planar identification with the chosen target is unique when it exists.

A surviving operation edge in \(t/E\) comes from a unique original edge not in \(E\): the original operation graph is a tree, so two collapsed components cannot be joined by two distinct original edges. Hence a further selected contraction set \(E'\) in the quotient lifts uniquely to a set \(\widetilde E'\) of surviving original edges. Define the composite to be contraction of \(E\cup\widetilde E'\). Its connected components are exactly the components obtained by the two successive collapses. Its external input order is the same. Thus it has the required target.

In a third contraction, lifting each final surviving edge through these quotients recovers that same original edge. In either parenthesization, the composite set is the union of the same three original sets. This proves associativity. The empty set is the identity. There are at most \(2^{V-1}\) contraction sets from any given source, and its targets form a finite object set, so all morphism sets and the category are finite.

Equation (C.44.2) gives \(h(t/E)-h(t)=|E|\). A nonidentity arrow strictly increases height, and no such arrow is an endomorphism. The height range is contained in \(0,\ldots,L-1\); this proves the chain bound. Parallel arrows are not identified: for example, in a chain of three unary operation vertices above one external leaf, contracting either one of the two operation edges gives the same two-unary-vertex shape. These two selected edge sets are different arrows.

Contracting all \(V-1\) operation edges gives a single operation vertex. Formula (C.44.1) gives that vertex arity \(n\), so the quotient is the \(n\)-corolla. This is the only selected set giving one remaining vertex. Thus the arrow to the corolla is unique from every object, proving terminality. For \(n=0\) it is the nullary vertex; for \(n=1\) it is the unary vertex. Neither is erased or identified with an external leaf.

For the augmented normalized nerve, append the unique arrow to the terminal corolla to a strict \(q\)-simplex not already ending there, with coefficient \((-1)^{q+1}\); send a simplex already ending there to zero. In augmented degree minus one send the generator to that terminal vertex. The boundary term deleting the newly appended vertex gives the original simplex. Every other boundary term cancels its counterpart after applying the homotopy to the old boundary, because composing an arrow with the unique terminal arrow is again that unique terminal arrow. If the original simplex ends at the terminal object, deleting that last vertex is the sole term restored by the homotopy. These calculations give \(\partial h+h\partial=1\), including the augmentation. They use uniqueness of the terminal arrow, not uniqueness of all arrows; the parallel morphisms are retained in every simplex. Appending stays in the same finite normalized chain complex because a maximal strict chain already ends at its terminal height.

Finally its endomorphism groups are trivial, its morphism sets are finite, and every nonisomorphism strictly raises the displayed height. It satisfies all the hypotheses of C.31.2, whose complete proof gives the projective relative bar resolution of length at most \(L-1\), with the actual parallel-arrow composition differential. This proves the last assertion. ∎

The lemma supplies the full finite index, including its unit vertices and parallel contractions. The next two theorems construct its actual grafting and native execution diagrams. Nerve contractibility alone is not substituted for those enhanced maps.

#### C.44.2. Grafting retains nullary vertices and unary seams

**Theorem C.44.2.1.** Let \(m\ge0\), \(n_1,\ldots,n_m\ge0\), and let the positive vertex capacities be \(L_0,L_1,\ldots,L_m\). Put \(N=\sum_i n_i\) and \(L=\sum_{i=0}^mL_i\). Literal planar grafting gives a functor
\[
 \mathfrak g:
 \mathcal T_{m,L_0}\times\prod_{i=1}^m\mathcal T_{n_i,L_i}
                   \longrightarrow\mathcal T_{N,L}.
 \tag{C.44.3}
\]
It sends every nonidentity morphism to a nonidentity morphism, preserves summed endpoint height jumps, and regroups associatively. Its actual reduced index bar map, after the tensor shuffle, is a chain coalgebra map retaining the parallel contractions. The statements and canonical common-input squares of C.42.1–C.43.1 consequently apply to these finite directed categories, even though they are not posets.

Grafting the one-corolla is compared with the identity by its *seam contraction*. It is not an equality of index objects. This comparison is natural and all its successive seam contractions have their original contraction-set coherence. A zero-input operation remains a nullary vertex throughout.

**Proof.** For \(m=0\), there are no inner trees and grafting is the identity on the outer zero-input tree. The empty product, summed height and index-bar map have that same identity interpretation. For \(m\ge1\), replace the \(i\)-th external input leaf of the outer tree by the root output of the \(i\)-th inner tree. The joining edge is an operation edge between its outer parent vertex and that inner root. Retain that seam edge and both its vertices. This is a planar rooted tree with \(N\) external leaves, and
\[
 V(\mathfrak g(t_0;t_1,\ldots,t_m))
                         =\sum_{i=0}^mV(t_i)\le L.
 \tag{C.44.4}
\]
The equality also holds when an inner tree has no external leaves: its operation root is still present and joined by its seam. The result always has an operation root.

Every original operation edge of each factor remains an operation edge in the graft. These embedded edge sets are disjoint from one another and from the new seams. On morphisms, embed each selected contraction set from its factor and take their union in the grafted tree. Collapsing that union gives exactly the graft of the factor quotients: no seam is selected, and each collapsed component lies inside its original factor. The ordered input edges of a quotient component agree before and after joining the seams. Thus this construction has the target asserted in (C.44.3).

For two successive morphisms, each surviving factor edge lifts to the same original factor edge and then to its same embedded graft edge. The union rule for composition in C.44.1 therefore agrees on both sides. Identity sets remain empty. This proves the functor equation, without identifying two different contractions merely because they have the same quotient shape. A nonidentity factor morphism contracts at least one embedded edge, so (C.44.4) shows that its image reduces the total vertex count. It is nonidentity.

With \(h_i=L_i-V(t_i)\) and \(h=L-V(\mathfrak g(t_i))\), (C.44.4) gives \(h=\sum_i h_i\) on the grafted objects. In particular the endpoint height jumps are exactly summed, including zero-size blocks.

Nested grafting in either order attaches the same operation vertices to the same external-input positions. Its original factor edges and its successive joining seams are the same edges, with the same planar order. This proves associativity of the object construction. The selected edge sets from all morphisms also have the same embeddings, so proves it on morphisms.

The linear index functor preserves identity arrows and takes nonidentity arrows to nonidentity arrows. Projection to the scalar identity categories therefore commutes with it on every mapping component. Its reduced bar map applies the functor to each suspended index letter. The original word endpoints remain composable; its coproduct is unchanged word cutting, and its differential composes adjacent arrows with the unchanged suspended signs. Functoriality of composition proves its chain equation. It is thus an actual colored chain coalgebra map, also when distinct source objects acquire the same grafted shape.

Precompose this map with the actual shuffle from the tensor of the factor index bars to the bar of their product category. The shuffle's word and root sign cancellations are C.34.2 and C.42.1; none uses uniqueness of an arrow between two objects. This gives the asserted map from the tensor index cores. A shuffle preserves total suspended degree and grafting preserves the summed height jump, so it preserves the height weight. Its regrouping identities are the original shuffle identities together with the literal associativity just proved.

We verify the stated extension of the common-input results. In each of these finite categories the nonidentity arrow span is an ideal, because every such arrow strictly raises height. The complement is the product of scalar identity lines. Each arrow line has degree zero and every composable nonidentity bar word has length at most the finite height range. These are exactly the properties used in C.42.1's full free-resolution, sign, minimal-model and weight proofs. Parallel arrow lines are separate basis coefficients in those same formulas; merging their letters uses their actual category composition. All those proofs therefore apply with the unchanged maps. C.43.1's canonical-unit naturality and shuffle naturality likewise use only the functor and coproduct identities, which have just been checked. In particular the input restriction remains \(g^{\otimes n}\otimes1_{\!D_{\mathcal T}}\), with no lost contraction label.

Let \(u\) be the one-corolla and \(t\) any formal tree. The tree \(\mathfrak g(u;t)\) has a new unary root and one new seam. Contract that seam to obtain \(t\); this is a nonidentity arrow reducing vertex count by one. Similarly inserting a one-corolla at an external leaf creates a unary vertex and its joining operation edge; contracting that edge removes it. Under any contraction in \(t\), the seam is still a distinct edge until it is selected. The union of the seam and the embedded old contraction set is the same in either order. This proves naturality.

For several inserted one-corollas, their seam edges are distinct. Contracting any selected subset gives the original selected-edge morphism; two orders of seam contraction lift to the same union of original seam edges, by C.44.1. This proves their higher index coherence. The statement is about those actual arrows, not about replacing the arrows by identities on a reduced bar. Their geometric functor images may be identities; C.43.2 retains those scalar outputs. Nullary vertices are neither external leaves nor unary identities and are never removed by the object grafting formula. ∎

#### C.44.3. Finite execution states and the native unit diagram

**Theorem C.44.3.1.** Fix a formal tree \(t\) with \(n\) external leaves and \(V\le L\) operation vertices. Its execution states are the subsets \(J\) of operation vertices closed under operation descendants: a vertex can be executed only after its operation children. They form a finite poset under inclusion, with height \(|J|\), initial empty state and terminal completed state.

The ordered frontier at state \(J\) has
\[
 m_J=n+\sum_{v\in J}(1-r(v)),\qquad
                0\le m_J\le n+|J|\le n+L.
 \tag{C.44.5}
\]
Executing a ready vertex of arity \(r\) changes this frontier by replacing its \(r\) consecutive factors with one, including insertion of the tensor unit when \(r=0\). The state index remains directed when this increases the frontier arity. Its chain length is at most \(V\).

Actual rational ordered convolution gives the coherent enhanced execution diagram on the finite additive envelopes of the categories \(\mathcal G_{\mathbf Q}^{\otimes m_J}\). Its step at that vertex is the corresponding convolution, the identity for \(r=1\), or the original unit functor for \(r=0\), with identity functors on the unchanged factors. Its state comparisons, formal tree contractions, unary seams and grafting maps are the actual finite-frame tensor, proper-composition and unit maps. They retain their higher enhanced components.

Finite input label pools have finite forward image-summand closures in this state diagram. Its represented kernel cohomology is nonnegative, even and degreewise finite on every resulting finite corner. All states with \(m_J=0\) use the genuine empty tensor input. After extending rational coefficients to \(E\), C.29's full enhanced ordered comparison acts coherently on this whole native diagram.

**Proof.** A subset closed under operation descendants is an order ideal of the finite child-before-parent partial order. The family of such subsets, including the empty and full subsets, is finite and closed under its stated inclusions. Each proper inclusion adds a vertex, giving the claimed height and chain bound.

Define its frontier by recursively traversing the original tree. At an already executed vertex, retain its output edge as one frontier factor and stop traversing its children. At an unexecuted vertex, traverse its ordered children. An external input leaf contributes its edge; an unexecuted nullary vertex contributes no factor. This produces an ordered list. It also specifies the insertion slot of a ready nullary vertex, even when the current frontier is empty.

For a ready vertex, each operation child is already executed, so its output edge is a frontier factor; its external-leaf children are frontier factors as well. They occur consecutively in their original input order. Their replacement by the vertex output removes \(r(v)\) factors and adds one. For a nullary vertex this inserts one factor at its traversal slot. Starting from the \(n\) external factors and executing any linear extension of \(J\) therefore proves the equality in (C.44.5). Nonnegativity also follows directly from the frontier definition. Since every \(r(v)\ge0\), that equality gives the upper bound. At the full state the frontier is the root output, so is one; this is also the edge-count identity (C.44.1).

This direction is execution height, not frontier arity. For example, two ready nullary children of a binary root give the successive arities \(0,1,2,1\); all three steps strictly increase \(|J|\). The initial empty input and the creation of unit factors are retained without a graph cycle.

At state \(J\), take its factors in the actual enhanced generator category, keeping their finite additive IC envelopes when a convolution decomposes. Execute a ready vertex by \(F_r\): \(F_1\) is the identity, \(F_0\) selects \(IC_0\), and \(F_r\) for \(r\ge2\) is the original derived ordered convolution. The empty tensor category is the coefficient generator category, with its ordinary perfect envelope; it is not identified with the full endomorphism category of \(IC_0\). The higher equivariant endomorphisms of that output still belong to its represented kernel.

For an inclusion \(J\subset K\), each new frontier output determines the operation subtree made from the vertices of \(K\setminus J\) below it, with frontier edges of \(J\) as its ordered input leaves. A surviving old frontier edge is an identity strand. These components form an ordered forest. Each old frontier input occurs exactly once among them, while a component can have zero inputs. Evaluate the components independently and take their ordered external product. This defines the actual partial functor \(F_{KJ}\) on the state input category.

For \(J\subset K\subset M\), the forest for \(M\setminus J\) is obtained by grafting the forests for \(M\setminus K\) and \(K\setminus J\); identity strands remain identities. Thus its functor comparison is the native grafting comparison. We give its geometric construction, including the zero-input components. The formal contraction comparisons below concern forest functors on their fixed input profiles. They do not assert a functor deleting an arbitrary factor from an intermediate category. A unit-born factor is selected by \(F_0\), while its full target mapping space remains in the represented kernel.

Replace every nullary vertex in that forest by one fixed input labelled \(IC_0\), retaining its position. The remaining positive-arity operations form an ordinary ordered convolution expression, with unary operations acting as identities. If there are \(a\) variable frontier inputs and \(c\) nullary vertices, its expanded ordered chain has \(a+c\) input factors. All endpoints and formal frames can be chosen at finite bounds for these finitely many inputs. The coefficient is the original descended external product, with \(IC_0\) at those fixed positions.

*Convolution and rigidity*, Theorem A.6.2.1 constructs the two unit maps on the identity correspondence and the associativity map from the common chain correspondence. Its proof uses the actual normalized descent, proper base-change and projection mates; in particular the group-dimension shifts cancel for an \(IC_0\) input. C.27.3 and C.33.1 retain those same kernels and maps on their complete enhanced finite envelopes. Consequently the expanded forest evaluation is the proper image of this actual common-chain coefficient, not a new functor chosen only on perverse objects.

If a contraction consumes a nullary child, the corresponding \(IC_0\) modification is trivial on that coefficient's support. The chain with this trivial step is identified with the chain with that step omitted. The normalized unit comparison is the actual identity-correspondence map just proved in Lesson 7; it leaves no residual shift. A unary seam uses the same identity comparison. The other contractions use the original proper-composition and derived tensor associativity maps. Thus every formal contraction in C.44.1, including two distinct contractions giving the same shape, is assigned its actual geometric comparison.

For a finite diagram of contractions, use the expanded chain of its original forest, inserting trivial steps when a quotient omitted them. On that common support the maps are compositions of those same tensor identifications, identity correspondences and proper counits. The source ordered tensor maps and proper-composition mates carry their original all-order coherence, as explicitly retained in C.27.3–C.33.1. Normalized enhanced torsor descent carries the whole diagram and its specified higher components to the generator envelope. This proves coherence for every state chain, interchange of two independent executions, unit seam and forest graft. It is the specified native resolution diagram throughout. No statement that an arbitrary enhanced natural-transformation space is contractible, or that its higher components vanish, is used.

In particular the two executions of independent ready vertices agree through the original tensor interchange comparison. When both are nullary, the final ordered frontier has both fixed \(IC_0\) factors in their original planar slots, regardless of which was created first. Their comparison is still the actual unit/tensor map. Resolving the native diagram records every higher state-chain component; C.31.2 bounds its relative index resolution by \(V\). If a corresponding index arrow has an identity as geometric image, C.43.2 uses its full scalar twisting output. It is not replaced by a reduced zero-arrow map.

Now choose finitely many input tuples. At each state, include the finite simple tuple summands of all already selected source tuples' forward images. Each operation is a perverse convolution on simple inputs, by the proved Satake exactness; the unit is perverse and the identity is exact. Its image is therefore a finite sum of simple IC objects, by C.33.1's arbitrary-characteristic-zero semisimplicity input. There are only finitely many states and inclusions. Their height increases, so this forward construction terminates at the completed state and adds only finitely many labels. It imposes no closure under an arbitrary tensor operation returning to an earlier state.

For a partial forest \(F_{KJ}\), its represented cohomology corner is the original mapping cohomology from \(F_{KJ}(\mathbf P)\) to a selected target tuple. That source is the finite sum just described. The target tensor mappings are finite balanced tensors of the IC mapping groups in C.33.1; their finite-sum and finite-tensor splitting proves they are nonnegative, even and degreewise finite. This applies also when the source tuple is empty: the output of a nullary vertex is \(IC_0\), and its actual higher mappings are retained. It proves the kernel assertion without treating the coefficient input as those larger equivariant endomorphisms.

Finally C.33.1's coefficient extension is the actual extension on these kernels, identity modifications, unit coefficient \(IC_0\), proper maps and coherent resolution diagrams. It therefore identifies the rational execution diagram extended to \(E\) with its native \(E\)-coefficient diagram. Apply C.29.3's full enhanced ordered comparison, with its specified unit, block and higher components, to each of the forests above. Strong ordered coherence gives the comparisons on their states, grafts, contractions and unit seams simultaneously. This establishes an actual enhanced comparison of the native diagram over \(E\). Its realization as one common-core bar coordinate, with complete product and cross-arity equation domains, remains the separate next construction; it is not inferred here from a set of independent one-step comparisons. ∎

#### C.44.4. Parallel unit contractions and changing frontier arity

**Exercise C.44.4.1.** Let a binary root have two nullary operation children and no external leaves. Compute the contraction category on this tree, its one-edge quotients and its terminal quotient. Why must its two one-edge arrows remain distinct even if both geometric functor components are the same unit isomorphism?

**Solution.** There are three operation vertices, two operation edges \(e_{\mathrm L},e_{\mathrm R}\), and external arity zero. Contracting the left edge or the right edge gives in each case a unary operation vertex above one nullary operation vertex. These are two different selected sets and therefore two parallel arrows. Contracting both gives the nullary zero-corolla, the terminal object. On a capacity-three stage their heights are respectively \(0,1,2\).

The source evaluation is \(IC_0*IC_0\); the one-edge evaluations use its left or right unit comparison before the final unary identity comparison. The two arrows retain those different native comparisons and their later coherence. Equality of their object components cannot remove one of the index arrows or its mixed mapping and higher resolution components. C.43.2 retains a scalar functor image for either arrow without identifying their input index letters.

**Exercise C.44.4.2.** For that same tree, list all execution states, their frontier arities and their two paths to the full state. Explain why the unit creation and the later convolution give a directed state graph, despite returning to a one-factor frontier.

**Solution.** Write \(\ell,r\) for the nullary children and \(b\) for the binary root. The states and arities are
\[
 \begin{array}{c|ccccc}
 J&\varnothing&\{\ell\}&\{r\}&\{\ell,r\}&\{\ell,r,b\}\\
 \hline
 |J|&0&1&1&2&3\\
 m_J&0&1&1&2&1 .
 \end{array}
 \tag{C.44.6}
\]
The paths execute either \(\ell,r,b\) or \(r,\ell,b\). Executing only \(b\) is forbidden until its two operation children have completed. In the right-first path, creating \(\ell\) next inserts its unit factor before the existing right factor, so the final two-factor order is still left then right.

Each step raises \(|J|\) by one. The final state and the one-child states are distinct even though their frontier arity is one. Thus their one-input cores are tagged by different execution states; no reverse arrow is added and no cycle arises. The completed evaluation is the original convolution of the two created units, with its native unit comparison. Its equivalence to a single unit is recorded by that comparison rather than by identifying the execution states.

![Formal nullary and unary vertices retain two different unit contractions with the same quotient shape; directed execution states create units while their frontier arity changes; the original expanded finite-frame unit and proper maps carry the native comparison diagram](assets/formal-unital-tree-indices.png)

Lemma C.44.1.1 proves the actual finite category with its parallel contraction arrows and terminal corollas. Theorem C.44.2.1 proves all-arity noncollapsing grafting, including zero inputs and unary seams. Theorem C.44.3.1 constructs the typed execution forests and their original enhanced unit/grafting diagram. Exercises C.44.4.1–C.44.4.2 give the displayed parallel-arrow relation and frontier diamond. Native unit maps are proved in Convolution and rigidity, Theorem A.6.2.1. Editable SVG source. Free background on the unital higher-component conventions: [Keller, Sections 3.5–3.6](https://arxiv.org/pdf/math/9910179).

### C.45. Canonical cobar projections and contracted kernel lifts

#### C.45.1. Surjectivity and relative lifting on free generators

Write \(C=B\mathcal M\), where \(\mathcal M\) is the strictly unital minimal positive generator category: its reduced mappings have degree at least two and its relative scalar category is split. Put
\[
 A_r=C^{\otimes r},\qquad R_r=\Omega A_r,\qquad
 U=\Omega C,\qquad U_r=U^{\otimes r}.
 \tag{C.45.1}
\]
The zero-fold categories are the coefficient field with its one empty-tuple object. We allow finite additive matrix envelopes, using the relative balancing of C.38.1.

**Theorem C.45.1.1.** The canonical map \(\kappa_r:R_r\to U_r\) of C.41.1 is surjective on graded mappings. Its kernel on each mapping complex is contractible. Suppose an object and scalar assignment and a strict dg functor \(P:R_s\to U_r\) are given. There is a strict dg lift \(\widetilde P:R_s\to R_r\), with the same object and scalar assignment, satisfying
\[
 \kappa_r\widetilde P=P.
 \tag{C.45.2}
\]
One may retain a previously given lift on a free dg subcategory generated by a specified, differential-stable collection of source generator summands. This includes previously specified full source corners. The construction can be made successively along nested corners, enlarging finite target pools to contain the previously chosen images. It asserts existence of compatible choices along that exhaustion, rather than naturality of arbitrary splitting choices under all maps.

**Proof.** A target graded monomial is an ordered tensor of words in the individual free generators \(t c_i\) of \(\Omega C\). At the current tuple of objects, the source generator
\(t(1\otimes\cdots\otimes c_i\otimes\cdots\otimes1)\)
maps to \(t c_i\) in that factor, with scalar identities in the other factors. Multiply these lifts, taking factor one first, then factor two, and so on. Their image is precisely the ordered pure tensor monomial. The endpoint tuples follow the endpoints of the factor words. Such monomials span every graded mapping, proving surjectivity. The argument retains all intermediate labels, works for matrix entries and is the identity for \(r=0\).

C.41.1 proves that \(\kappa_r\) is a quasi-isomorphism on these mapping complexes. For completeness its surjective kernel \(K\) is acyclic without requiring a long-exact-sequence citation. If \(z\in K\) is closed, injectivity on cohomology gives \(z=dv\) in the source. The element \(\kappa_r v\) is closed. Surjectivity on cohomology gives a closed source element \(w\) with \(\kappa_r v-\kappa_r w=db\). Lift \(b\) graded to \(\widetilde b\). Then \(v-w-d\widetilde b\) belongs to \(K\) and still has differential \(z\). Thus \(K\) is acyclic. The splitting proof of C.30.1 supplies an endpoint and coefficient-linear contraction \(h_K\), with
\(d h_K+h_Kd=1\) and \(h_K^2=0\). A graded coefficient-linear section \(\sigma\) of \(\kappa_r\) exists by that same splitting proof.

Filter a reduced element of \(A_s\) by the total number \(\ell\) of original bar letters in its \(s\) factors. Every source free generator \(t a\) has \(\ell\ge1\). Since \(\mathcal M\) is minimal, the internal bar differential has no unary term and its nonzero terms reduce \(\ell\). In a proper coproduct split, both factors have strictly smaller total length. Hence the generator differential (C.39.15) is a sum of generators and products of generators already defined at smaller length. This is the needed triangular statement; it does not claim that a split reduces the sum of the lengths of its two factors.

Assume the lift is defined on those lower lengths. For a homogeneous generator \(x\), take \(v=\sigma P(x)\) and form
\[
 o_x=dv-\widetilde P(dx)\in K,
 \qquad \widetilde P(x)=v-h_Ko_x.
 \tag{C.45.3}
\]
It belongs to \(K\) because \(P\) is a chain map and the lower-length lifts already satisfy (C.45.2). It is closed because the lower-length lift is a chain map and \(d^2x=0\). Therefore \(d h_Ko_x=o_x\), proving the required differential equation for the new image. Its projection is still \(P(x)\). These choices are linear on a whole generator summand: its differential, \(\sigma\) and \(h_K\) are linear. Extend multiplicatively from the free relative generators. The chain equation on generators and scalars then proves it on every product by the dg Leibniz rule. Induction defines the lift on the direct-sum cobar; there is no infinite series on an element.

For a prescribed free dg subcategory keep its generator images and perform the construction on a coefficient-linear complement of its generator summands. The differential-stability hypothesis and the same induction establish compatibility. A full source corner, constructed from its own bar category, embeds by retaining precisely its allowed endpoint and intermediate labels. Its generator collection is differential-stable, so it is one of these subcategories. Along a nested exhaustion retain the already assigned images, pass to larger target pools containing them, and repeat. Every earlier generator remains fixed. No independently chosen contractions on unrelated corners are identified. On finite pools the positive bar and cobar degree bounds of C.34.1 and C.39.4 make each degree finite; every chosen image is a finite combination. Extending the chosen rational sections and contractions to a field extension preserves all identities.

When \(s=0\) there are no reduced source generators and the supplied scalar assignment is already the lift. When \(r=0\), \(\kappa_0\) is the identity and the supplied \(P\) is the lift. A nullary convolution with target arity one selects \(IC_0\) in \(U\); it retains that object's full mapping complex. It is not a replacement of \(\operatorname{End}(IC_0)\) by the zero-fold coefficient field. ∎

#### C.45.2. A fixed projection and its entire module kernel

**Theorem C.45.2.1.** Let \(\widetilde P:R_s\to R_r\) be a lift in C.45.1. For tuple or finite additive objects set
\[
 M(y,x)=\operatorname{Hom}_{R_r}(\widetilde P x,y),\quad
 Q(y,x)=\operatorname{Hom}_{U_r}(P x,\kappa_r y),\quad
 p:M\longrightarrow Q.
 \tag{C.45.4}
\]
Here \(p\) is induced by \(\kappa_r\). Pull their ordinary represented graph modules back to the same left core \(L=A_r\) and right core \(A=A_s\), using the canonical bar units. After undoing the cross suspension by (C.41.6), their cofree bicomodules are \(Y_M=L\otimes M\otimes A\) and \(Y_Q=L\otimes Q\otimes A\), with their full module differentials. The fixed map
\[
 \phi=1\otimes p\otimes1:Y_M\longrightarrow Y_Q
 \tag{C.45.5}
\]
